(d) The amended rules govern RIFs in which the agency **issues** the RIF notice **on or after September 2, 2026**. Q2.answer:
Ratings window: notices issued Sept. 3, 2026, so the relevant period is the four years before that date (Sept. 3, 2022–Sept. 3, 2026); no cutoff date. Values: Level 5 = 7, Level 4 = 5, Level 3 = 3, Level 2 = 0, Level 1 = 0 (5 CFR 351.503(a)(1)).

(a) **Performance credit, veterans’ points, totals (5 CFR 351.503, 351.504):**
- **Abbott** (career → competitive service tenure subgroup I; no preference, Subgroup B): 7+5+5 = **17**; +0 = **17**.
- **Bianchi** (career, Subgroup I; preference eligible with 30%+ compensable disability): 5+0+3 = **8**; +5 (351.504(a)(1), Subgroup AD) = **13**.
- **Castillo** (career, Subgroup I; retired lieutenant colonel, 22 years, retired pay based on length of service, no disability): 7+5+5 = **17**; **not a preference eligible** under 351.504(b) — (b)(1) fails (no disability retirement), (b)(2) fails (pay based on 20+ years), (b)(3) fails, and (b)(4) requires a disabled veteran who also meets (b)(1)–(3) — so +0 (Subgroup B) = **17**.
- **Dalton** (career, Subgroup I; preference eligible, no disability): two ratings only = 7 and 0; proxy for the missing rating = (7+0)÷2 = **3.5** (351.503(f)(2)); performance credit = 7+3.5 = **10.5**; +3 (351.504(a)(2), Subgroup A) = **13.5**.
- **Eze** (four-year term appointment, probation completed; not career/career-conditional): not excluded from competition — the exclusions in 351.202(d) reach only temporary/time-limited appointments of one year or less, initial probationers, and Schedule C/G employees — so she is a competing employee in competitive service tenure subgroup II (351.502(a)(3)): 5+5+5 = **15**; +0 (Subgroup B) = **15**.
- **Fontaine** (career, Subgroup I; no preference): one rating only = 5; 5×3 = **15** (351.503(f)(3)); +0 = **15**.

(b) **Order of retention (highest→lowest):**
1. **Abbott 17** (Subgroup I)
2. **Castillo 17** (Subgroup I) — tied with Abbott at 17; both in subgroup I, so the tie is broken by service computation date, earliest first: Abbott (May 1, 2003) ahead of Castillo (Aug. 1, 2012) (351.501(c)).
3. **Fontaine 15** (Subgroup I)
4. **Eze 15** (Subgroup II) — tied with Fontaine at 15; the tie is broken by tenure subgroup, I ahead of II (351.501(c)), so Fontaine ranks ahead of Eze; service dates are not reached.
5. **Dalton 13.5** (Subgroup I)
6. **Bianchi 13** (Subgroup I)
**Released (two lowest): Bianchi and Dalton.** (Bianchi is released despite the 5-point 30% disability augmentation because 13 is still the lowest total.)

(c) **Under the earlier rules Bianchi would have stood *above* Abbott.** Under the pre-2026 rules employees were ranked first by tenure group (I, II, III), then within each tenure group by veterans’-preference subgroup (AD, A, B), and only then by years of service as augmented by performance credit (adjusted SCD). Because both are tenure group I career employees, Bianchi’s subgroup AD outranks Abbott’s subgroup B before any consideration of performance or length of service; the old rules also allowed a Group II preference eligible to be released ahead of a Group I non-veteran, which OPM illustrates and criticizes. Performance played no role until employees were already inside the same tenure-group/veterans-subgroup category.

(d) **What Bianchi may see (5 CFR 351.506):** as an employee who received a specific RIF notice she may review (herself or through a representative acting for her) the **complete retention register** for her competitive level, including the names of all other employees listed, each employee’s performance credit as augmented by veterans’ preference, and each employee’s service computation date — so that she can see how the competitive level was constructed and how relative standing was determined — plus the **complete registers for other positions** that could affect the composition of her competitive level and/or her assignment rights. The agency must keep registers/records for at least two years after it issues the notice, and access must be consistent with FOIA and the Privacy Act. Employees who have not received a specific notice have no right under this section to review the registers.
Q2.basis: 5 CFR 351.501 (order of retention; tie-breakers), 351.502 (tenure groups/subgroups), 351.503(a)(1), (c)(1), (f)(2), (f)(3) (performance credit, ratings used, proxies), 351.504(a), (b) (veterans’ points; retired members), 351.506 (records and inspection), 351.202(d) (exclusions), all as revised by 2026-15665 at 91 FR 49218–49223; earlier rules described in the preamble at 91 FR 49181–49183 (tenure group → vets subgroup AD/A/B → adjusted SCD; Group II preference eligible can be released before a Group I non-veteran) and 91 FR 49198–49201 (current-rule examples and adjusted-SCD arithmetic).
Q2.uncertainty: The arithmetic for Dalton depends on 351.503(f)(2) producing a .5 proxy (3.5); the rule expressly contemplates a “.5 decimal value,” so no rounding is authorized. Eze’s status assumes her term appointment was for more than one year (four years, per the facts) and that she is in the competitive service; the documents do not print 5 CFR part 316 subpart C, so that classification rests on the exclusion language in 351.202(d)(2)(iii), which reaches only temporary appointments of one year or less under subpart D.

Q3.answer:
(a) All five are career employees and retired members with no continuous covered civilian employment since 1964, so the deciding provision is 5 CFR 351.504(b) (as revised by 2026-15665), with 351.504(a) for points/subgroup:
- **A (Lt. Col., 22 years, retired pay based on length of service, no disability): not a preference eligible.** (b)(1) fails (retirement is not based on disability); (b)(2) fails (retired pay is based on 20+ years); (b)(3) fails (not employed since Nov. 30, 1964); (b)(4) is unavailable because he is not a disabled veteran as defined in 5 U.S.C. 2108(2). **0 points; Subgroup B** (351.504(a)(3)).
- **B (Commander, 21 years, retired pay based on length of service, 40% compensable disability): not a preference eligible.** (b)(1) fails (the retirement is based on length of service, not disability); (b)(2) fails (pay based on 20+ years); (b)(3) fails; (b)(4) requires a disabled veteran who *also* meets one of (b)(1)–(3), which he does not; (b)(5) (age 60, 10 U.S.C. ch. 67) is inapplicable on these facts. **0 points; Subgroup B** (351.504(a)(3)).
- **C (Major, 14 years, disability retirement for injury in the line of duty as a direct result of armed conflict, 60%): preference eligible** under **(b)(1)(i)**; his rank/status also satisfies (b)(4). Disability of 30% or more → **5 points; Subgroup AD** (351.504(a)(1)).
- **D (Master sergeant, 24 years, retired pay based on length of service, no disability): not a preference eligible.** (b)(1) fails (no disability retirement); (b)(2) fails (pay based on 20+ years); (b)(3) fails; (b)(4) is officer-rank-specific and in any event requires a disabled veteran. **0 points; Subgroup B** (351.504(a)(3)).
- **E (Staff sergeant, medical retirement after 16 years for a training injury not from armed conflict or an instrumentality of war, 10%): preference eligible** under **(b)(2)** — his retired pay is *not* based on 20 or more years of full-time active service ((b)(1) fails because the injury was not a direct result of armed conflict nor caused by an instrumentality of war). Disability under 30% → **3 points; Subgroup A** (351.504(a)(2)).

(b) **Employee A:** appointed Sept. 7, 2010 with no earlier civilian service. Because he is a retired member covered by 351.504(b), 5 CFR 351.505(b)(2) limits his military credit to (i) active service during a war or in a campaign/expedition for which a campaign or expedition badge was authorized (he is not a preference eligible, so (b)(2)(ii) is unavailable). Two campaign years are creditable, all other active duty is not: SCD = Sept. 7, 2010 − 2 years = **September 7, 2008** (351.505(d)(1)–(2)).
**Employee C:** appointed the same day, but he *is* a preference eligible under 351.504(b), so 351.505(b)(2)(ii) gives him credit for his **total** active service (14 years): SCD = Sept. 7, 2010 − 14 years = **September 7, 1996**.

(c) **The AD/A/B subgroups play no role in the order of retention.** Under the amended rules standing within a tenure group is set by performance credit as augmented by the preference points (5 points for 30%+ disabled, 3 for other preference eligibles, 0 otherwise); the subgroup label is only an identifier recorded/shown on the register (351.504(a)) and disclosed in the notice (351.802(a)(2)). Ties are broken by tenure subgroup and then by service computation date, not by veterans’ subgroup (351.501(b)–(c)); OPM states that the old categorical subgroup structure is replaced and that preference now operates through numerical augmentation of performance credit.
Q3.basis: 5 CFR 351.504(a)–(b), 351.505(b)(2), (d), 351.501(b)–(c), 351.802(a)(2), as revised by 2026-15665 at 91 FR 49221–49223, 49226; preamble explanations at 91 FR 49181–49183 (preference implemented by points; subgroups replaced) and 91 FR 49200–49202 (worked examples).
Q3.uncertainty: 5 U.S.C. 2108 and pre-2026 5 CFR 351.504 are not printed in these documents; the analysis rests entirely on the text of 351.504(b) as amended. The reading that 351.505(b)(2) applies to *every* retired member covered by 351.504(b) (not only to those who are preference eligibles) follows the words “who is covered by Sec. 351.504(b)”; the alternative reading — that only preference eligibles under that provision are limited — would give A credit for all 22 years (SCD September 7, 1988). The question’s inclusion of exactly two campaign years indicates the limited reading is intended.

Q4.answer:
All computations apply 5 CFR 351.503 (as revised by 2026-15665): values 7/5/3/0/0 for Levels 5/4/3/2/1; the three most recent ratings of record received in the four-year period before either the notice date or the agency cutoff; proxy for two ratings; ×3 for one rating; ratings must be issued with signatures **and** on record.

(a) **Farah — performance credit 13.** Notices Sept. 3, 2026; the four-year window is Sept. 3, 2022–Sept. 3, 2026, so all five ratings qualify. The three most recent are Aug. 10, 2026 (Level 5 = 7), Nov. 14, 2025 (Level 3 = 3), Nov. 15, 2024 (Level 3 = 3): 7+3+3 = **13**. (The two older Level 4 ratings are not used; only three ratings count.)

(b) **Cutoff date = July 20, 2026; credit = 13.** Thirty days before Sept. 3, 2026 is **July 20, 2026** (Sept. 3 − 30 days; July has 31 days, so Sept. 4→31 days back…30 days back = July 20). Ratings on or before the cutoff and within four years before it (July 20, 2022–July 20, 2026) are: Nov. 18, 2022 (Level 4 = 5), Nov. 20, 2023 (Level 4 = 5), Nov. 15, 2024 (Level 3 = 3); the Nov. 14, 2025 and Aug. 10, 2026 ratings fall after the cutoff and are excluded (351.503(c)(2)). Sum: 5+5+3 = **13**.

(c) **No, it cannot be used.** A rating counts only if it was issued with all reviews and signatures **and** is “on record (i.e., … available for use by the office responsible for establishing retention registers)” (351.503(c)(3)). The July 15, 2026 rating was signed and given to the employee before the July 20 cutoff, but it was not entered in the system used by the office that builds the registers until Aug. 15, 2026 — after the cutoff, and the cutoff bars ratings “put on record” after that date (351.503(c)(2)). Both conditions must be met by the cutoff.

(d) **Gina — performance credit 12.** Notices Sept. 3, 2026 (no cutoff), so the window is Sept. 3, 2022–Sept. 3, 2026. The Aug. 15, 2022 Level 5 falls **outside** the window. Two ratings remain — Nov. 15, 2024 (Level 4 = 5) and Nov. 14, 2025 (Level 3 = 3): proxy = (5+3)÷2 = **4**; credit = 5+3+4 = **12** (351.503(f)(2)).

(e) **Hank — performance credit is based on the “modal rating,” not zero.** Because he has no rating of record in the four-year period (his prior organization’s ratings are not treated as ratings of record, and 351.503(b)(3) leaves that equivalence determination to the agency’s sole discretion), 351.503(f)(1) requires that his credit “be based on the modal rating as defined in Sec. 351.203 for the summary level pattern that applies to the employee’s official position of record at the time of the reduction in force.” The numeric answer therefore depends on that modal rating: if the modal rating under the applicable five-level pattern is Level 3 (3 points), the credit is 9 if the modal rating is substituted for all three ratings, or 3 if it is substituted only once.
Q4.basis: 5 CFR 351.503(a)(1), (b)(3), (c)(1)–(4), (f)(1)–(3), as revised by 2026-15665 at 91 FR 49220–49222; the cutoff must be specified in the agency’s issuance (351.503(c)(2), (c)(4)(ii)).

(1) 351.503(f)(1) cross-refers to a “modal rating” definition in 5 CFR 351.203, but the 2026 rule’s amendatory instructions to 351.203 neither add nor print that definition, so its content cannot be verified from the Federal Register; and the text does not say whether the modal rating replaces one rating or all three, so Hank’s exact credit cannot be computed from the documents. Q5.answer:
(a) Lee (no preference, SCD 3/2/1998) has ratings 3/3/3; Park (no preference, SCD 7/8/2019) has 5/5/5. Both are career employees (tenure subgroup I) and Subgroup B.
**New rules** (5 CFR 351.501(b)): Lee = 3+3+3 = **9**; Park = 7+7+7 = **21**; Park has higher retention standing, so **Lee is released** and Park is retained.
**Earlier rules:** the register was ordered by tenure group, then veterans’ subgroup (both are Group I/B), then “years of service as augmented by performance credit,” i.e., the service computation date adjusted backward by additional service credit derived from the ratings, earliest adjusted date first. OPM’s published examples supply the credit for exactly these rating patterns: 3/3/3 = **12 years** and 5/5/5 = **20 years**. Lee: 3/2/1998 − 12 years = **3/2/1986**. Park: 7/8/2019 − 20 years = **7/8/1999**. Lee’s adjusted date is earlier, so under the earlier rules **Park is released** and Lee is retained.
- (i) Notices **Aug. 28, 2026** (RIF effective Oct. 27, 2026): the notice predates Sept. 2, 2026, so the RIF is processed under the earlier rules (2026-15665 DATES; 91 FR 49206–07). **Park is released**, Lee retained (arithmetic above). The RIF’s October effective date is irrelevant.
- (ii) Notices **Sept. 2, 2026**: the rule applies to a notice issued “on or after” Sept. 2, 2026, so the amended rules apply. **Lee is released** (9 vs. 21).
- (iii) Notices **Sept. 3, 2026**: amended rules apply. **Lee is released** (9 vs. 21).

(b) **No — retention standing is not recalculated.** Retention standing is fixed as of the date the employee **receives** the specific RIF notice (5 CFR 351.507(a)), here Sept. 3, 2026. The amended 5 CFR 351.805(b) expressly provides that an amended notice issued solely to state a later effective date “is not a new specific reduction in force notice for purposes of Sec. 351.507 and does not require the agency to redetermine or recalculate retention standing under subpart E,” while preserving the duty to correct an error under 351.507(c). Lee’s Oct. 15 rating (after the notice) is therefore not counted; Lee remains released on the Sept. 3 standings, subject only to correction of any error.

(c) The three events are different:
1. **Which version of the rules applies — the date the agency *issues* the RIF notice.** “An agency that issues a RIF notice on or after the effective date must apply the RIF provisions as amended”; a pre-Sept. 2 notice is processed under the old rules (2026-15665 DATES, 91 FR 49178; Implementation Considerations, 91 FR 49206–07).
2. **The end of the four-year ratings period — the date the agency *issues* RIF notices, or the agency-established cutoff date, if any** (5 CFR 351.503(c)(1)–(2), (c)(4)(i), 91 FR 49221).
3. **The employee’s tenure subgroup and retention standing — the date the employee *receives* a specific RIF notice** (5 CFR 351.502(a)(2)–(3), (b)(2)–(3); 351.507(a), 91 FR 49220, 49223).
Q5.basis: 2026-15665: DATES (91 FR 49178), Implementation Considerations (91 FR 49206–07), 5 CFR 351.501, 351.502, 351.503(c), 351.507, 351.805(b) (91 FR 49219–49223, 49226); earlier-rules ordering and adjusted-SCD arithmetic described at 91 FR 49181–49183, 49198–49201 (including worked examples giving 12 years for 3/3/3 and 20 years for 5/5/5).
Q5.uncertainty: The old rules themselves are not printed in the Federal Register (the pre-2026 text of 351.501–351.504 is superseded); the adjusted-SCD result for (i) rests on the preamble’s description and its examples, which supply 12 and 20 years for these exact rating patterns but do not state the underlying formula as regulatory text. The premise that both employees are in the same competitive area/level and that neither has an exception available is assumed.

Q6.answer:
(a) **Assignment rights (5 CFR 351.701 as revised):** because Jordan’s current annual rating of record is Level 2 (minimally satisfactory) and he is a competitive-service tenure-group employee, he is entitled to an offer of assignment rather than furlough or separation. The offered position must require no reduction, or the least possible reduction, in representative rate; must be in the **same competitive area**; must have the **same type of work schedule**; and must be a position held by another employee with **lower retention standing in the same tenure group** that is **not more than three grades (or three appropriate grade intervals) below** his position (five grades for a 30%+ disabled preference eligible), for which he is qualified (351.701(a)–(b), 351.702, 351.703). His position is in a one-grade interval progression, so three grades below GS-13 = GS-12, GS-11 and GS-10 (351.701(b)(2), (d)(1)–(2), using only the released employee’s grade progression).
- **1. GS-12 (Ellis, lower standing): available — and this is the position the agency must offer**, because it involves no reduction in representative rate (351.701(a)).
- **2. GS-11 (Frank, lower standing): available** (second interval), but not the offer, since GS-12 is available.
- **3. GS-10 (Gale, lower standing): available** (third interval), but not the offer.
- **4. GS-9 (Hana, lower standing): not available** — four grades below GS-13, beyond the three-grade limit.
- **5. GS-12 (Ito, higher standing): not available** — the position must be held by an employee with *lower* retention standing.
- **6. GS-12 part-time (Kim, lower standing): not available** — the offered position must have the same type of work schedule (full-time) as the position from which he is released (351.701(a)).
- **7. GS-12 in a different competitive area (Lund, lower standing): not available** — the offered position must be in the same competitive area (351.701(a)).

(b) **If Jordan is a preference eligible with a compensable service-connected disability of 30 percent or more:** the grade limit becomes **five grades** (351.701(b)(2)), so **GS-9 (Hana)** also becomes available. The agency must still offer **GS-12 (Ellis)** — the least possible reduction in representative rate; the extra grade range only expands the pool if the higher positions were unavailable. (If pay bands were involved, 351.701(f) would allow an equivalent band or up to two bands lower for such an employee.)

(c) **If Jordan’s current annual rating of record is Level 1 (Unacceptable): he has no assignment rights at all.** 351.701(a) extends the right only to a released employee “with a current annual performance rating of record of minimally satisfactory (Level 2) or equivalent, or higher.” He would be furloughed or separated (subject to any exception); no position on the list must be offered.

(d) **If Jordan and all seven holders are in the excepted service:** subpart G assignment rights do not apply. 5 CFR 351.705(a) lets an agency, at its discretion, adopt provisions giving excepted-service competing employees assignment rights against other positions under the same appointing authority on the same basis as 351.701. Unless this agency has adopted such provisions, **Jordan has no assignment right to any of the seven positions** and could be separated without an offer; if the agency has adopted 351.705(a) provisions, the analysis in (a)–(c) would apply by the terms of that issuance.

(e) **Both statements in the old handbook are out of date.** (i) *Bumping and retreating* were replaced by a single assignment right: a released employee may be assigned to a position held by an employee with lower retention standing in the same tenure group, within the grade limits, for which he is qualified; OPM states that the separate concepts of “bumping” another employee in a lower subgroup and “retreating” to a lower-ranked employee’s position in the same subgroup are no longer needed and that this eliminates successive rounds of bumping/retreating (91 FR 49202). (ii) The rule that a Level 2 employee could not obtain assignment to a position held by an employee with a higher performance rating (former 5 CFR 351.701(d)) was **eliminated**; OPM concluded the restriction is no longer necessary now that performance dominates the register. So a Level 2 employee is not barred by the other employee’s higher rating; he is barred only by his own Level 1 (no rights at all) or by the structural limits in 351.701 (standing, grades, area, schedule).
Q6.uncertainty: The documents do not print 5 CFR 351.703 (quality/qualification ranking) or the pre-2026 text of 351.701(d); their content is taken from OPM’s description. “Appropriate grade intervals” for a one-grade interval progression are read as three one-grade steps (GS-12/11/10); the preamble and the rule refer to the grade progression of the released employee’s position but do not work a one-grade-interval example. Part (d) assumes the agency has not adopted a 351.705(a) issuance; the facts do not say.

Q7.answer:
(a) **The Merit Systems Protection Board hears the appeal.** The OPM RIF appeals rule applies only to a RIF action for which the agency issues a specific RIF notice **on or after September 2, 2026** (2026-15666, DATES, 91 FR 49230). Morgan’s notice was issued Aug. 31, 2026, so her RIF is processed under the old part 351 (2026-15665 DATES, 91 FR 49178; 91 FR 49206–07), under which 5 CFR 351.901 granted MSPB appeal rights. The MSPB’s 2026 rule removes RIF appeals from 5 CFR 1201.3 but states that it will not apply the amendment to pending cases or newly filed cases relating to agency actions taken before Sept. 2, 2026, will accept RIF appeals where the agency’s RIF notice was issued before the rule’s effective date, and will not dismiss them on the ground that OPM’s rule displaced its jurisdiction (2026-16456, DATES and § I.B, 91 FR 51997). Documents bearing on the answer: **2026-15665** (DATES/implementation), **2026-15666** (DATES), **2026-16456** (DATES, I.B, III). The Aug. 25, 2026 correction **2026-17338** corrects only typographical/citation errors in the appeals rule and does not change its applicability.

(b) **OPM hears the appeal.** The notice (Oct. 19, 2026) is after Sept. 2, 2026, so the OPM process governs (2026-15666 DATES; 5 CFR 351.901(a) as revised, 91 FR 49263). **How to file:** she (or her representative) must file through **OPM’s electronic filing system identified on OPM’s website**; OPM will not accept pleadings, evidence or documents by e-mail or postal mail absent a showing of good cause and OPM approval (351.902(a)), and parties must register as e-filers (351.902(c)). **Deadline — Tuesday, January 19, 2027, 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.** Counting under 351.902(b): the appeal must be filed within **30 calendar days from the effective date** (Dec. 18, 2026); the first day counted is the day after the effective date (Dec. 19 = day 1), so day 30 is **Jan. 17, 2027** (Dec. 19–31 = 13 days; Jan. 1–17 = 17 days; 13+17 = 30). Jan. 17, 2027 is a **Sunday**, so the period includes the first workday after that date; Monday, Jan. 18, 2027 is **Martin Luther King, Jr. Day** (a Federal holiday), so the first workday is **Tuesday, Jan. 19, 2027**. Timeliness requires electronic filing by 11:59 p.m. ET that day (351.902(b), (b)(1)).

(c) **What she must prove:** by a preponderance of the evidence — (1) that her written appeal is timely; (2) that OPM has jurisdiction; (3) that the agency **failed to comply with an applicable statute or OPM regulation** governing RIF actions under part 351; and (4) that the failure **prejudiced** her by causing the appealed action or the loss of a “materially more favorable outcome” (351.901(b), 91 FR 49263). **Hearing:** she is not entitled to one. Review must be based **solely on the developed written record** unless OPM determines that a hearing is “necessary and efficient,” which is defined as a record insufficiently developed on a material fact or a material disputed issue of witness credibility (351.905(c), 91 FR 49265).

(d) **The rule bars the grievance route.** 5 CFR 351.901(c)(2): a RIF action taken under part 351, “and any matter relating to an appeal of such an action, may not be raised under a negotiated grievance procedure or contested through grievance arbitration,” and (c)(1) makes the subpart I procedures the sole and exclusive means of appealing (91 FR 49263–64, as corrected by 2026-17338). **What the preamble says about existing agreements:** OPM states that the final rule “does not retroactively invalidate existing CBAs or purport to adjudicate particular CBA disputes,” that it does not adopt the position that the proposal would “automatically vitiate existing agreements mid-term,” and that when agreements are renegotiated the governmentwide rule will limit agencies’ duty and ability to bargain for a conflicting RIF appeal process; questions about particular existing agreement provisions, negotiability, or unfair-labor-practice allegations “remain matters for resolution under chapter 71 by the appropriate forum” (91 FR 49245). OPM grounds this on 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1) and IRS v. FLRA and, separately, does not displace collateral matters within EEOC, IG, MSPB, DOL VETS or OSC jurisdiction (351.901(c)(3)).

(e) **No.** 5 CFR 351.901(c)(4): “A party cannot obtain judicial review of a decision under this subpart” (91 FR 49264). There is also no further administrative appeal of OPM’s final decision (351.909(e)).

(f) **Yes — she may still appeal, by Friday, April 9, 2027.** 5 CFR 351.902(b)(3) provides that if, before the appeal filing period expires, the employee timely filed a complaint, appeal or other matter within the independent jurisdiction of an entity listed in 351.901(c) (which includes the Office of Special Counsel), and the final decision on that matter materially affects her retention standing, order of release, assignment rights or other rights under part 351, she “may file an appeal under this subpart within 30 calendar days after the date on which the decision on that matter becomes final and is no longer subject to further administrative review.” Her OSC complaint was filed before the (Dec. 18, 2026-based) filing period expired and produced a final decision on **March 10, 2027** that would have changed her retention standing. Counting: March 10 + 30 days = **April 9, 2027** (Mar. 10→Mar. 31 = 21 days; Apr. 1–9 = 9 days; 21+9 = 30). April 9, 2027 is a Friday, so no weekend/holiday extension is needed. OPM decides in its sole and exclusive discretion whether the collateral decision materially affects her rights, so the appeal should be filed by that date and should document the effect on standing.

(g) **The provision that decides between (a) and (b) is the applicability (DATES) paragraph of the RIF appeals rule:** “This final rule applies only to a RIF action for which an agency issues the employee a specific RIF notice under 5 CFR 351.802 on or after September 2, 2026” — published at **91 FR 49230** (2026-15666). It is reinforced by the main rule’s DATES paragraph (“An agency that issued a RIF notice before the effective date of the rule must process the RIF under the regulations in effect when the RIF notice was issued,” 91 FR 49178) and by MSPB’s rule (91 FR 51997–98). The event that separates (a) from (b) is therefore the date the agency **issued** the specific RIF notice (Aug. 31 vs. Oct. 19), not the separation date.
Q7.uncertainty: The pre-2026 text of 5 CFR 351.901 is not printed (it is described, not reproduced, in 2026-16456 at 91 FR 51997). The Jan. 19, 2027 deadline assumes the Federal holiday schedule (Jan. 18, 2027 = Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr.) and that 351.902(b)(1)'s “first workday after that date” language is applied by skipping a holiday Monday; the rule does not spell out a holiday-on-the-first-workday scenario. In (f), OPM’s discretionary “materially affects” determination is a second condition she must satisfy in addition to timeliness.

Q8.answer:
(a) **Version in force today (through Nov. 17, 2026):** 5 CFR 351.806 is the version that predates 2026; the main RIF rule (2026-15665) did **not** amend it (its subpart H instructions touch only 351.802 and 351.805, 91 FR 49226), and the 2026 amendment to 351.806 does not take effect until Nov. 18, 2026. OPM describes that current text as directing agencies to keep a RIF-affected employee “in duty status during a RIF notice when possible,” with an emergency paragraph (now carried forward as (c)) under which, in an emergency lack of work or funds, the agency may place the employee on annual leave with or without consent, leave without pay with consent, or in a nonpay status without consent (91 FR 65933, 65936; proposed rule 91 FR 39034). The full current text is not reproduced in any 2026 Federal Register document.
**Version adopted but not yet in force:** 2026-21320, 91 FR 65939, revising 351.806 in full, **effective November 18, 2026**: “§ 351.806 Status during notice period. (a) General. Under ordinary circumstances, an employee will remain in a duty status during the notice period. (b) Administrative leave. Nothing in this section precludes an agency from placing an employee on administrative leave for all or part of the notice period when the agency determines that such leave is appropriate and the use of administrative leave is consistent with part 630, subpart N, of this chapter. (c) Emergency lack of work or funds. When, in an emergency, the agency lacks work or funds for all or part of the notice period, it may place the employee on annual leave with or without the employee’s consent, on leave without pay with the employee’s consent, or in a nonpay status without the employee’s consent.”

(b) **Consent is not required, and there is no express duration limit.** Neither adopted 351.806(b) nor its companion leave provision conditions RIF notice-period administrative leave on employee consent — consent appears only in 351.806(c) for leave without pay. The companion provision, new 5 CFR 630.1403(c)(10), lists as an acceptable use “administrative leave to employees subject to an involuntary separation via a reduction in force (RIF) during the period between receipt of the RIF notice and the RIF separation when the agency determines it is in the Government’s best interests” (91 FR 65940); it states no maximum number of days. The only durational guidance is the general principle in 630.1403(a)(3) that administrative leave is for “brief or short periods … usually for not more than 1 workday,” with longer periods allowed in the circumstances described in paragraph (c) or when the agency otherwise determines appropriate — and note that the extended-period examples (c)(9) and (c)(11) are expressly “[s]ubject to Governmentwide limits established by OPM and agency limits,” whereas (c)(10) contains no such clause. Practice under 630.1403(a)(2), (a)(4), (a)(5) (agency policy, higher-level approval where the use/amount is not authorized by written policy) still applies, and administrative leave remains discretionary, not an entitlement.

(c) **Before the adopted text takes effect, OPM says its policy guidance already allowed it.** OPM states that the regulatory clarification “is consistent with OPM policy guidance which already provided that an authorized agency official may provide administrative leave between an employee’s receipt of a notice of involuntary separation and the effective date of that separation,” citing section D.1.b of the OPM memorandum “Template for Agency Administrative Leave Policies” (CPM 2025-12, July 30, 2025) (91 FR 65926 & n.3). The proposed rule made the same point, noting that keeping a RIF-affected employee in duty status “when possible” may not be possible where the agency is concerned about jeopardizing Government interests (91 FR 39034). OPM also stresses that the change does not waive, suspend or displace any part 351 requirement: “The only change made to part 351 is to Sec. 351.806” (91 FR 65926).

(d) **No.** OPM states that the new 630.1403(c)(10) and revised 351.806 “address only whether an employee may be placed in a paid, non-duty status during a RIF notice period” and “do not alter the substantive or procedural requirements governing RIF, which continue to apply in full,” and that nothing in the rule authorizes bypassing RIF competition, retention registers, or appeal rights (91 FR 65926). Consistently: retention standing is determined as of the date the employee receives the specific RIF notice and is not affected by later duty status (5 CFR 351.507(a)); the notice must still contain the 351.802 content; records must be preserved and are inspectable by the employee (351.506); and the appeal rights in subpart I (OPM) are unaffected. Administrative leave also cannot be used to satisfy the Government-obligation temporary exception (5 CFR 351.608(c) prohibits administrative leave under part 630, subpart N).
Q8.basis: 2026-21320: 91 FR 65925–26 (responses to comments; policy guidance CPM 2025-12), 65933 (§ M, duty-status presumption), 65936 (emergency annual leave paragraph), 65939–40 (5 CFR 351.806 text; 630.1403(a)(3), (c)(9)–(11)); 2026-13073, 91 FR 39034 (proposed rule, “when possible”); 2026-15665, 91 FR 49226 (no amendment to 351.806) and 5 CFR 351.507, 351.506, 351.608(c), 351.802.
Q8.uncertainty: The exact current text of 5 CFR 351.806 (in force through Nov. 17, 2026) is not printed in any 2026 Federal Register document; the description above is OPM’s own characterization plus the language it says it is replacing (“when possible”). No provision states a maximum length for RIF notice-period administrative leave; the interaction between 630.1403(a)(3)’s “usually … not more than 1 workday” guidance and (c)(10) is not addressed expressly.

Q9.answer:
RIF noticed October 13, 2026 → the amended rules apply (notice on/after Sept. 2, 2026: 2026-15665 DATES, 91 FR 49178).

**Step 1 — does not comply.** A competitive area may be established by an organizational unit on the agency’s official chart, designated/approved by the agency head or a designee at or above headquarters level (satisfied here), and must be clearly distinguished as to operation, work function, staff and supervisory oversight (351.402(b)(1)). But where an agency “establishes or materially modifies a competitive area within 90 days before issuing specific reduction in force notices,” it “shall submit a description of the competitive area, along with a written statement explaining the bona fide organizational basis … to OPM for approval in advance of the reduction in force” (351.402(c), 91 FR 49219). Aug. 17 to Oct. 13, 2026 is 57 days, within 90. **Required:** submit the description and bona fide-basis statement to OPM for approval in advance (and make descriptions/explanations readily available for review).

**Step 2 — in order.** A career-conditional employee serving an initial probationary period is not a “competing employee” (351.202(d)(2)(ii)), and the agency “may retain such an employee while releasing a competing employee” without determining retention standing, applying the order of release, or providing assignment rights (351.202(d)(3)).

**Step 3 — does not comply.** 351.203 defines “Initial probationary period” as the 5 CFR 11.2 probationary period and expressly excludes “the probationary period applicable on initial appointment to a supervisory or managerial position described in subpart I of part 315.” OPM says a career-tenured supervisory probationer “would be included in the RIF … and would not be subject to the exclusion” (91 FR 49191). **Required:** rank Ms. Ortiz on the retention register for her competitive level as a competing employee in competitive service tenure subgroup I (351.502(a)(2)).

**Step 4 — does not comply.** A 30-day cutoff before an Oct. 13, 2026 notice is **September 13, 2026**; after that date “no new ratings of record will be put on record and used for purposes of this subpart,” and credit is based on the three most recent ratings received in the four years before the cutoff (351.503(c)(2)). The Oct. 2, 2026 rating is after the cutoff. **Required:** exclude it, even though it raised Mr. Pruitt’s score; using it for one employee also violates the uniform-and-consistent-application requirement (351.503(c)(4)).

**Step 5 — does not comply.** With two actual ratings (Level 5 = 7 and Level 4 = 5) the missing rating is filled by a **proxy**: (7+5)÷2 = **6**, so the credit is 7+5+6 = **18**, not a presumed Level 3 and not 15 (351.503(f)(2)); the Level 3 presumption appears nowhere in the rule.

**Step 6 — does not comply.** Extra points for performance are permitted only under 351.503(d) (single pattern) — and only where the agency’s appraisal system’s highest summary level is a level “3” — or under 351.503(e) (multiple patterns, by transmutation). Here all employees are rated on one five-level pattern, so no additional points may be added; a written policy cannot supply authority the regulation withholds. **Required:** compute credit solely under 351.503(a) (7/5/3/0/0).

**Step 7 — in order.** When competing employees in the same level have identical performance credit as augmented by veterans’ preference, are in the same tenure subgroup and have identical service dates, “the agency may select any tied employee for release” (351.601(c), 91 FR 49223); 351.501(c) likewise produces a tie.

**Step 8 — does not comply.** 5 CFR 351.602 (as revised) provides that an agency “may not release a competing employee from a competitive level while retaining in that level an employee with: (a) A specifically limited temporary or term promotion” (91 FR 49223). Mr. Reyes’ temporary promotion ending March 2027 is exactly that. **Required:** do not release the competing employee while retaining him; end/curtail the temporary promotion or defer the release.

**Step 9 — in order.** No assessment is required where, “during the 5-year period ending on the date the employee receives a specific reduction in force notice,” the employee “occupied the same position, or a position at the same grade or pay level with substantially the same duties, occupational series, qualification requirements, and conditions of employment, and received a rating of record of Level 3, Fully Successful, or higher … for performance of those duties” (351.702(a)(4)(v), 91 FR 49226). Mr. Silva held the same position until 2023 and had a Level 4 rating for it in 2022 — inside the five years ending Oct. 13, 2026. (The provision is permissive, so an assessment would also have been permissible.)

**Step 10 — does not comply.** An assessment “must not consist solely of, or principally rely on, an automated self-assessment” (351.702(a)(4)(iii)); it must allow demonstration of job-related skills, be based on a job analysis, and be one of the acceptable types (structured interview, work-related exercise, structured resume review, etc.) (351.702(a)(4)(i)–(ii), (iv)). **Required:** use a job-analysis-based, skills-demonstrating assessment.

**Step 11 — does not comply.** Each 351.608 exception “stands alone and may not be sequenced or stacked in combination with another exception”; if more than one is available the agency may apply the exception giving the longest retention (351.608(a)(3)). The undue-interruption exception is capped at **90 days** (351.608(b)) and the general “other exceptions” exception at up to **90 days** (351.608(g)). **Required:** a single exception — at most 90 days under (b) or up to 90 days under (g) — not 60 + 60; and for an exception longer than 30 days the agency must notify higher-standing employees reached for release and annotate the register (351.608(a)(4)).

**Step 12 — does not comply.** For a notice issued Oct. 13, 2026 the appeal lies to **OPM**, not MSPB: 5 CFR 351.901(a) (as revised), and 351.802(a)(6) requires the notice to state the employee’s right to appeal to OPM, “the time limit for filing an appeal under Sec. 351.902(b) … and the electronic filing system, identified on OPM’s website, through which an appeal must be filed” (2026-15666, 91 FR 49263; MSPB jurisdiction over RIF appeals was removed by 2026-16456, 91 FR 51997). The 30-calendar-day-from-effective-date period itself is correct (351.902(b)), but the forum and the required e-filing information are not.
Q9.uncertainty: Step 9 assumes the 2022 Level 4 rating covered performance of the duties of the position he held until 2023 (the facts so state) and that the position he was offered is the same position he held; if the offered position differed in series/grade/duties the exception would not apply. Step 11 assumes the agency is invoking the 351.608(b) undue-interruption exception and 351.608(g); the 90-day caps are maxima, and the rule does not say whether a single (b) exception may be followed later by a fresh (g) exception after the retained period ends — only that they may not be “sequenced or stacked” for the same retention.

Q10.answer:
(a) **On September 10, 2026, paragraph (1) of the definition of “displaced” in 5 CFR 330.602 contained only its introductory text, with no subparagraphs (i) or (ii):** “A current competitive service employee in the competitive service tenure group at grade GS-15 (or equivalent) or below (or another qualifying competitive service appointment, as determined by OPM) who:”. Paragraphs (1)(i) and (1)(ii) — the substantive descriptions of when an employee is “displaced” — had been **removed** from the Code of Federal Regulations as of Sept. 2, 2026. **Why:** amendatory instruction 11 of the RIF final rule (2026-15665, 91 FR 49217) directed that paragraph (1) “be revised” but set out only the introductory text as the revised text; as published, that instruction had the effect of deleting (1)(i) and (1)(ii) (2026-18800, 91 FR 58363).

(b) **What changed, when, by which document:** the definition was restored by **2026-18800, “Reduction in Force; Correction,” 91 FR 58363–58364, published and effective September 15, 2026**, which revises paragraph (1) in its entirety — restating the introductory text as revised by the final rule and **restoring (1)(i) and (1)(ii) as they read before the final rule**. It also confirms that the revision to the “surplus” definition was published as intended and is unaffected. **Reason for acting without notice and comment:** OPM found good cause under **5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)** (and, for immediate effect, 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)) because the document “makes no substantive change to the regulations” — it restores regulatory text in effect before Sept. 2, 2026 that OPM did not propose to remove and that the final rule never discussed removing. **How OPM characterized it:** as a correction of a clerical/amendatory-instruction error — an inadvertent removal of two paragraphs that left the definition “incomplete”; the corrections are “non-substantive.”

(c) **After the change:** restored (1)(i) makes an employee “displaced” if she “[r]eceived a reduction in force (RIF) separation notice under part 351 of this chapter and has not declined an offer under part 351, subpart G, of this chapter of a position with the same type of work schedule and a representative rate at least as high as that of the position from which the employee will be separated” (5 CFR 330.602(1)(i), as restored at 91 FR 58363–64).
- **Offer with a lower representative rate, declined: Nadia is still “displaced.”** The disqualifying declination is only of an offer with “a representative rate at least as high as” her present position; a lower-rate offer is not such an offer, so declining it does not affect her status (and, under 351.701(a), a position with a lower representative rate would in any event not have been the offer the agency was obliged to make while a same-rate position was available).
- **Offer with the same representative rate, declined: she would not be “displaced”** — assuming the work schedule was full-time (the “same type of work schedule” as her full-time position). Declining a same-schedule, same-or-higher-representative-rate assignment takes her outside (1)(i).
Q10.basis: 5 CFR 330.602 (definition of “displaced,” paragraph (1)), as amended by 2026-15665 instruction 11 (91 FR 49217) and restored by 2026-18800 (91 FR 58363–64, including the restored text of (1)(i)–(ii)); 5 CFR 351.701(a) (lease-reduction offer rule).
Q10.uncertainty: The pre-2026 text of 330.602 is not printed; the restoration is “as they read before the final rule” per OPM. Whether a particular offer is “the same type of work schedule” is a fact question; the answer assumes both positions are full-time. Note also that the CTAP definition is only about CTAP eligibility; it does not itself confer or deny assignment rights under 351.701.

Q11.answer:
Comparing the amendatory text of the proposed rule (2026-04377, 91 FR 10926–10934) with the amendatory text of the final rule (2026-15665, 91 FR 49215–49226), the real differences (ignoring punctuation, capitalization, and citation *format*) are:

1. **5 CFR 351.202(d) introductory text.** Proposed: “Employees excluded. The provisions of this part do not apply to the following categories of employees.” Final: “Employees excluded from reduction in force competition. An employee holding one of the following appointments is not a ‘competing employee’ for purposes of a reduction in force.”
2. **351.202(d)(1)(ii) and (d)(2)(i)–(ii) — timing of probation/trial status.** Proposed: exclusion for “an employee serving a trial period **as of the date the agency issues a specific reduction in force notice**” and for indefinite/career-conditional employees “serving an initial probationary period **as of the date the agency issues a** reduction in force notice.” Final: the “as of the date the agency issues a specific reduction in force notice” qualifier is **deleted** in all three places (“An employee serving a trial period”; “An employee serving under an indefinite appointment who is serving an initial probationary period”; “A career-conditional employee serving an initial probationary period”).
3. **351.202(d)(2)(iii) — competitive-service temporary appointments.** Proposed: “An employee serving on a temporary **or term** appointment of 1 year or less under subpart **C or D** of part 316.” Final: “An employee serving under a **temporary** appointment of one (1) year or less under subpart **D** of part 316.”
4. **351.202(d)(3) — consequences of exclusion.** Proposed: excluded employees “may be retained, furloughed, separated, demoted or reassigned **without regard to the provisions of this part**.” Final: the agency may retain them while releasing a competing employee and may furlough, separate, demote, or reassign “for a reason described in Sec. 351.201(a)(2) without determining the employee’s retention standing under subparts D and E …, applying the order-of-release provisions in subpart F …, or providing assignment rights under subpart G …, provided the action is otherwise consistent with the terms of the employee’s appointment and applicable law.”
5. **351.202(d)(4) — new paragraph.** The proposal had none; the final adds the requirement of a written notice under 351.801 for excluded employees who are furloughed more than 30 days, separated, demoted or reassigned (unless the action is merely expiration of a temporary/time-limited appointment), specifying which 351.802(a)/(b) content must and need not be included.
6. **351.203 — “Furlough.”** Proposed retained the clause “and is instead dependent entirely on congressional action, rather than agency action” at the end of the emergency-shutdown exclusion; the final **deletes** that clause.
7. **351.203 — “Rating of record.”** Proposed cites the summary-level pattern in “Sec. 430.208(**d**)”; final cites “Sec. 430.208(**e**)” — a change in which paragraph is cross-referenced (reflecting the July 7, 2026 republishing of 430.208). Proposed also reads “prepared at the end of an appraisal period **assessing** performance”; final reads “**for** performance.”
8. **351.203 — new definition “Restoration protected employee.”** Not in the proposal; the final adds it (a competing employee restored/reemployed after uniformed service who, as of the date of a specific RIF notice, remains entitled under 353.209(b) to retention for 6 months or 1 year).
9. **351.204 — Responsibility of agency.** Proposed: agencies are responsible for following and applying the regulations. Final adds “and for ensuring that such regulations are administered and applied consistent with all applicable laws, including the merit system principles set forth in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b).”
10. **351.302(d) — separation of an employee who declines to transfer.** Proposed: the losing agency “must use the adverse action procedures found in part 752 of this chapter.” Final: “must use the adverse action procedures found in **5 CFR part 752, if applicable, or other procedures required by law, regulation, or the terms of the employee’s appointment**.”
11. **351.402 — paragraph (c) added.** Proposed amended only paragraph (b); the final adds a new paragraph (c) requiring OPM approval (description plus written bona fide-basis statement submitted in advance) when a competitive area is established or materially modified within 90 days before specific RIF notices, and requiring that descriptions and explanations be readily available for review.
12. **351.502 — issue date vs. receipt date.** Proposed repeatedly used “as of the date the agency **issues** a specific reduction in force notice” (subgroup I, subgroup II, excepted subgroup I and II); the final replaces it with “as of the date the employee **receives** a specific reduction in force notice” in all four places (a)(2), (a)(3), (b)(2), (b)(3).
13. **351.502(a)(3) — competitive-service subgroup II.** Proposed excluded those “serving an initial probationary period or a temporary **or time-limited** appointment of 1 year or less under subpart **C or D**”; final excludes those “serving an initial probationary period or a temporary appointment of 1 year or less under subpart **D** of part 316.”
14. **351.503(a)(1).** Proposed: patterns “in Sec. 430.208(**d**)” and “0 for a Level 2 (**Minimally Successful** or equivalent)”; final: “5 CFR 430.208(**e**)” and “Level 2 (**Minimally Satisfactory** or equivalent).”
15. **351.503(b)(2) — internal cross-reference.** Proposed required use of summary levels “in accordance with **Sec. 351.501** (as augmented …)”; final says “in accordance with **paragraph (a) of this section** (as augmented …).”
16. **351.503(d) and (e)(1) — pattern citation and added historical clause.** Proposed cited “Sec. 430.208(**d**)”; final cites “Sec. 430.208(**e**)”; and final adds to (d) the parenthetical “**(i.e., a pattern A ‘pass/fail’, or pattern D system authorized under 430.208(d) prior to the final rule prescribed at 91 FR 41521)**,” with a parallel addition in (e)(2) (“as authorized under Sec. 430.208(d) of this chapter, as in effect prior to the final rule published at 91 FR 41521 (July 7, 2026))”).
17. **351.504(a)(1)–(3) — mandatory vs. precatory subgroup labeling.** Proposed: employees “**should** be identified as being in veterans’ preference Subgroup AD/A/B”; final: “**must** be identified.”
18. **351.505(b)(2) — wrong cross-reference corrected.** Proposed: “a retired member of a uniformed service who is covered by **Sec. 351.503(b)**”; final: “**Sec. 351.504(b)**.” (This changes which provision governs the creditable-service limits for retired members.)
19. **351.506(d) — added sentence.** Final adds: “This paragraph does not limit any right of access available under another statute or regulation.” The proposal had no such sentence.
20. **351.604 — the proposal’s furlough amendments were not adopted.** Proposed instruction 29 would have revised 351.604(b) (letting agencies set furlough/recall criteria by operational need and factors rather than by retention standing) and removed 351.604(d). The final rule contains **no amendment to 351.604** (OPM declined to finalize; see preamble, 91 FR 49202).
21. **351.605 — structure and wording.** Proposed put everything in paragraphs (a) and (b): “may use this **paragraph (a)**,” “when invoking this **paragraph (b)**,” included the notice content inside (b), and said the agency “**may** not apply assignment rights”; final restructures into (a) appropriate use, (b) abolishment, (**c) Notice** (cross-referencing 351.801 and identifying the competitive area being abolished), and **(d) Retention register not required** (“is not required to rank … and **must not** apply assignment rights”).
22. **351.606(a) — rewrite and corrected cross-reference.** Proposed: “When an agency applies Sec. 351.601, it shall give retention priorities over other competing employees to each competing employee entitled under **Sec. 351.209(b)** to retention for, as applicable, 6 months or 1 year after restoration.” Final: a six-paragraph provision keyed to both 351.601 **and 351.605**, fixing ordinary standing first and then applying a mandatory exception; if no other employee may be released (e.g., entire competitive area abolished) the employee may not be separated by RIF during the protection period and must be reassigned, with OPM placement assistance if the agency is abolished (38 U.S.C. 4314; 353.110); it adds limits ((a)(5)(i)–(iii)) and a documentation requirement ((a)(6)), and corrects the reference to **Sec. 353.209(b)**.
23. **351.608(a)(2) — CTAP cross-reference.** Proposed cited “part 330, subpart **E**” for the Career Transition Assistance Plan; final cites **subpart F**.
24. **351.608(e)(1)(ii) — description of employees outside 351.606(b).** Proposed: “because the employee is covered by a Federal leave system under an authority other than 5 U.S.C. chapter 63, the employee is covered by a retirement law not referenced in Sec. 351.606(b), or is covered by a health benefits law other than 5 U.S.C. chapter 89.” Final compresses this to “because the employee is covered by a Federal leave system under an authority other than 5 U.S.C. chapter 63, a retirement law not referenced in Sec. 351.606(b), or a health benefits law other than 5 U.S.C. chapter 89.”

Q12.answer:
(a) **Retention register for the GS-13 level.** Notices issued and received Oct. 5, 2026; no cutoff date, so the window is Oct. 5, 2022–Oct. 5, 2026. Values: 7/5/3/0/0 (5 CFR 351.503(a)(1)). All are in the competitive service tenure group (351.501(a)).
- **Alvarez** (career, no preference, Subgroup B): 7 (11/15/2023) + 7 (11/14/2024) + 5 (11/13/2025) = **19**; +0 = **19**. Subgroup I.
- **Brandt** (career, 30%+ disabled preference eligible): 3 + 5 + 0 = **8**; +5 (351.504(a)(1)) = **13**. Subgroup AD, tenure subgroup I.
- **Chen** (career, no preference): her Level 2 rating of Sept. 30, 2022 falls **outside** the four-year window. Two ratings count: 7 (11/14/2024) + 5 (11/13/2025); proxy = (7+5)÷2 = **6**; credit = 7+5+6 = **18** (351.503(f)(2)); +0 = **18**. Subgroup I.
- **Dube** (career-conditional, initial probation completed in 2025 → **tenure subgroup II**, 351.502(a)(3); preference eligible, no disability): two ratings only: 5 (11/14/2024) + 5 (11/13/2025); proxy = **5**; credit = 5+5+5 = **15**; +3 (351.504(a)(2)) = **18**. Subgroup A, tenure subgroup II.
- **Estrada** (career, preference eligible, no disability): the Level 5 rating received **Oct. 20, 2026** is after the Oct. 5 notice and is not within the four years before issuance, so it is not used. Three most recent in the window: 5 (11/15/2023) + 3 (11/14/2024) + 5 (11/13/2025) = **13**; +3 = **16**. Subgroup A, tenure subgroup I.
- **Farouk** (career, no preference): one rating in the window (11/14/2024 Level 3 = 3); credit = 3 × 3 = **9** (351.503(f)(3)); +0 = **9**. Subgroup I. He is also a **restoration protected employee** (see (b)).
- **Quinn: not on the register.** A career-conditional employee appointed March 2, 2026 who is still serving her initial probationary period is not a “competing employee” (351.202(d)(2)(ii)); the agency may retain her while releasing competing employees (351.202(d)(3)).
**Order of retention:** 1 **Alvarez 19**; 2 **Chen 18** (Subgroup I); 3 **Dube 18** (Subgroup II) — Chen and Dube tie at 18 and the tie is broken by tenure subgroup, I ahead of II (351.501(c)), so service dates are not reached; 4 **Estrada 16**; 5 **Brandt 13**; 6 **Farouk 9**.

(b) **Released from the GS-13 level: Estrada, Brandt, and Dube.** The three lowest-ranked employees are Farouk (9), Brandt (13) and Estrada (16) — but **Farouk may not be released**. He was restored to his position under 5 CFR part 353 on July 13, 2026 after 14 months of uniformed service; because the period of service exceeded 180 days he is entitled to one year of post-restoration retention protection (through July 13, 2027), so at the Oct. 5, 2026 notice date he was a “restoration protected employee” (351.203) and 351.606(a) requires a **mandatory exception**: the agency must determine his ordinary standing first (done: 9), then may not release him “before the expiration of the applicable retention protection period if another competing employee may be released instead,” and must document the exception and the employee released because he was passed over (351.606(a)(2), (a)(6)). Passing him over, the agency releases the next lowest three: **Estrada (16), Brandt (13), and Dube (18)** — i.e., Dube is released, and Chen and Alvarez are retained. (If Farouk were not protected, the three released would be Farouk, Brandt and Estrada.)

(c) **Offers of assignment (5 CFR 351.701):** each released GS-13 employee is entitled to assignment to a position held by another employee with lower retention standing in the same (competitive service) tenure group, not more than three grades below (five for a 30%+ disabled preference eligible), in the same competitive area, with the same work schedule, for which qualified, and involving no reduction or the least possible reduction in representative rate. The four lower positions’ holders’ standings (same window, three ratings each): Gomez GS-12 = 7+5+5 = **17**; Hill GS-11 = 5+3+3 = 11, +3 = **14**; Jones GS-10 = 5+5+5 = **15**; Ikeda GS-9 = 3+3+3 = **9**.
- **Dube (18; 3-grade limit):** positions with lower standing are Gomez (17), Hill (14), Jones (15) and Ikeda (9); grades within three of GS-13 are GS-12, GS-11 and GS-10. Least possible reduction → **GS-12 (Gomez)**. Not GS-11/GS-10 (a greater reduction is unnecessary); not GS-9 (more than three grades below).
- **Estrada (16; 3-grade limit):** Gomez (17) has **higher** standing, so no right to GS-12; Hill (14) and Jones (15) are lower. Least possible reduction → **GS-11 (Hill)**. Not GS-10 (greater reduction); not GS-12 (higher-standing holder); not GS-9 (beyond three grades).
- **Brandt (13; 30%+ → 5-grade limit):** Gomez (17) and Hill (14) and Jones (15) all have **higher** standing, so his only target with lower standing within five grades is **GS-9 (Ikeda)**. He receives that offer. (If he were not 30% disabled, GS-9 would be four grades below and unavailable — he would have no assignment right at all.)

(d) **If every offer is accepted, the employees separated from the agency are Gomez, Hill and Ikeda.** Dube is assigned to Gomez’s GS-12 position; Estrada to Hill’s GS-11; Brandt to Ikeda’s GS-9. Gomez, Hill and Ikeda are thereby released from their competitive levels, and because each “is qualified only for the position they hold,” none is qualified for any other position and none can be placed by assignment (351.701(a), 351.702) — each is separated. Alvarez and Chen keep their GS-13 positions; Quinn remains but is not part of the RIF competition (351.202(d)(2)(ii), (d)(3)); Farouk remains by the mandatory exception (351.606(a)); Jones is untouched. So the GS-13 level loses three positions and the agency loses three employees (Gomez, Hill, Ikeda), while no GS-13 employee is separated.
Q12.basis: 5 CFR 351.501, 351.502, 351.503(a)(1), (c)(1), (f)(2)–(3), 351.504(a), 351.202(d)(2)(ii), (d)(3), 351.203 (“Restoration protected employee”), 351.606(a)(1)–(6), 351.701(a)–(b), 351.702, as revised by 2026-15665 at 91 FR 49218–49226; USERRA protection periods and the 6-month/1-year rule described at 91 FR 49203 (38 U.S.C. 4316(c)); earlier example arithmetic at 91 FR 49200–49201.
Q12.uncertainty: Two points are not free from doubt. (1) Farouk’s exact protection period depends on 5 CFR 353.209(b), which is not printed; OPM’s preamble states the periods implement 38 U.S.C. 4316(c) (1 year for service over 180 days), and the facts give 14 months, so a 1-year period through July 13, 2027 is the only reading supported. (2) If an employee displaced by an assignment (Gomez, Hill, Ikeda) were qualified for other positions, successive assignment rights could displace others; the facts foreclose that by saying each is qualified only for the position held. The analysis also assumes no discretionary exceptions are used and that all positions are full-time and in the same competitive area.

Q13.answer:
Three places where the preamble of 2026-15665 describes the rule differently from the amendatory/regulatory text printed in the same document:

1. **Which section the erosion-of-duties change amends, and the triggering event (180 days vs. adverse effect on retention standing).** Preamble: “OPM is modifying **Sec. 351.201(a)(2)** to remove from the list of actions that require agencies to use RIF procedures reclassification of an employee’s position due to erosion of duties if the action would take effect after an agency had formally announced a RIF in the employee’s competitive area and **the RIF would take effect within 180 days**” (91 FR 49190); repeated: reclassifications “will take effect after an agency has formally announced a RIF … **that will take effect within 180 days**” (91 FR 49191). Text: the amendment is to **5 CFR 351.202(c)(3)**, and the exception contains **no 180-day element** — the bar applies to a reclassification “between the time an agency has formally announced a reduction in force in the employee’s competitive area and the completion of the reduction in force **where the reclassification action would adversely affect an employee’s retention standing** in the announced reduction in force” (instructions 18, 91 FR 49218–49219). **Another passage states it correctly:** the same page’s discussion of the anti-manipulation safeguard says the rule “will bar agencies from undertaking an erosion-of-duties reclassification between the formal announcement and completion of a RIF **if the action would adversely affect an employee’s retention standing**” (91 FR 49191), as does Executive Summary item 8 (91 FR 49178).

2. **Whether the competitive-service subgroup II exclusion covers “term” (and time-limited) appointments.** Preamble: “Competitive service tenure subgroup II will consist of every other competitive service employee who, as of the date of the RIF notice, is not serving an initial probationary period **or a temporary or term appointment of 1 year or less**” (91 FR 49196); similarly the Executive Summary says the rule excludes “temporary or time-limited appointments of one year or less” (91 FR 49178, item 2). Text: **5 CFR 351.502(a)(3)** as adopted excludes only “a **temporary** appointment of 1 year or less **under subpart D of part 316**” (91 FR 49220), and 351.202(d)(2)(iii) is likewise limited to temporary appointments of one year or less under subpart D (91 FR 49218). **Another passage states it correctly:** the preamble’s account of the final rule’s changes says the final rule “**removes a proposed reference to term appointments under part 316 subpart C**, making clear that the competitive-service temporary-appointment exclusion is limited to temporary appointments of 1 year or less under part 316 subpart D” (91 FR 49191), and the 351.202(d) discussion at 91 FR 49191–49192 describes only temporary appointments.

3. **What 5 CFR 351.602 continues to prohibit — “temporary appointment” vs. “temporary or term promotion.”** Preamble: “OPM is also modifying Sec. 351.602 to **remove the prohibition on retaining an employee serving a specifically limited temporary appointment** in a competitive level while releasing a competing employee from that level” (91 FR 49202). Text: 351.602 as revised still prohibits releasing a competing employee while retaining in that level an employee with “(a) A specifically limited **temporary or term promotion**” (91 FR 49223) — the retained prohibition concerns a temporary or term *promotion*, not a temporary *appointment*, and the reference to a temporary *appointment* is gone precisely because the prohibition that remains is different. **No other passage of the preamble corrects this one**; the only other description is the unexplained statement that OPM is “modifying Sec. 351.601 … [and] 351.602” (91 FR 49202).
Q13.basis: 2026-15665: preamble at 91 FR 49178 (Exec. Summary items 2 and 8), 49190–49191 (erosion of duties), 49196 (subgroup II), 49202 (351.602); amendatory text at 91 FR 49218–49220 (351.202(c)(3), (d), 351.502) and 49223 (351.602).

Q14.answer:
**(i) Preamble statements in OPM’s appeals rule that differ from its regulatory text (as published or as corrected):**
1. **“Part 351” vs. “this subpart” in the exclusivity clause.** Preamble: “Final Sec. 351.901(c) states that the procedures **in part 351** are the sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action …” (91 FR 49243; similarly “The final text continues to provide that **part 351** procedures are the sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action,” 91 FR 49230). Regulatory text as published: “The procedures in **this part** are the sole and exclusive means …” — corrected by 2026-17338 (91 FR 54796) to “The procedures in **this subpart** are the sole and exclusive means of appealing a reduction-in-force action taken under this part” (5 CFR 351.901(c)(1), 91 FR 49263).
2. **Effect on existing collective bargaining agreements.** Preamble: the rule “**does not retroactively invalidate existing CBAs** or purport to adjudicate particular CBA disputes,” OPM “does not adopt” the position that the proposal would “automatically vitiate existing agreements mid-term,” and “when agreements are renegotiated, this governmentwide rule will limit agencies’ duty and ability to bargain …” (91 FR 49245). Regulatory text: an unqualified prohibition — “A reduction-in-force action taken under this part, **and any matter relating to an appeal of such an action, may not be raised under a negotiated grievance procedure or contested through grievance arbitration**” (351.901(c)(2), 91 FR 49264), with no grandfathering of existing agreements.
3. **“Consolidating” the untimely-filing rule.** Preamble: “It also **consolidates the untimely-filing rule in Sec. 351.902(b)(2)** …” (91 FR 49230). Text: the final rule retains **two** untimely-filing provisions — 351.902(b)(2) (appeal “will be dismissed as untimely … unless the employee demonstrates good cause”) **and** 351.903(f) (“Untimely filings may be accepted upon a party’s showing of good cause at the sole and exclusive discretion of OPM”) (91 FR 49264–65).

**(ii) Changes from the proposed appeals rule (2026-02576, 91 FR 5874–77) to the final appeals rule that the final rule’s summary of changes (91 FR 49230–32) does not acknowledge:**
1. **5 CFR 351.906(b) and new (c).** Proposed: “When a party … fails to comply with a directive issued under paragraph (a), OPM **shall**, except when prohibited by law: [three sanctions]” (91 FR 5876). Final: OPM “**may**” impose them, **and** a new paragraph (c) requires that “[a]ny sanction … be proportionate, causally related to the violation, and no broader than necessary to protect the adjudicatory process” (91 FR 49266). The summary’s “Refining protective-order authority” bullet addresses only paragraph (a) (91 FR 49231).
2. **5 CFR 351.802(a)(6) — deletion of the MSPB service cross-reference.** Proposed: “The employee’s right, as applicable, to appeal to OPM. **The agency must also comply with Sec. 1201.21 of this title**” (91 FR 5874). Final: the right to appeal to OPM, “including the time limit for filing an appeal under Sec. 351.902(b) of this part and the electronic filing system, identified on OPM’s website, through which an appeal must be filed” — with no Sec. 1201.21 requirement (91 FR 49263). The summary mentions only the additions (91 FR 49230–31).
3. **5 CFR 351.905(c) — what OPM may do beyond the written record.** Proposed: review “based solely on the developed written record unless OPM determines that a **hearing or any other appropriate action** is necessary and efficient … and directs the parties to participate in such hearing or comply with such action” (91 FR 5876). Final: “unless OPM determines that **a hearing** is necessary and efficient in resolving an appeal” (91 FR 49266). The summary’s audit/investigation bullet discusses the narrowed audit standard and representative participation but not the elimination of “any other appropriate action” (91 FR 49231).
4. **5 CFR 351.902(c)(2) — e-filer exemption.** Proposed: “[n]o party may electronically file any document with OPM or access an appeal … unless registered as an e-filer” (91 FR 5875). Final adds “**or exempted under paragraph (c)(7) of this section for good cause**” (91 FR 49264). The summary discusses exemptions only in the context of the (c)(7) good-cause provision and sanctions (91 FR 49231).

**(iii) Inconsistency about which RIF appeals the Board will still hear:**
1. **Three different triggers within the Board’s rule.** The DATES paragraph says the Board “will not apply this rule to pending cases or to newly filed cases relating to **agency actions taken before the effective date** of OPM’s rulemakings, and will continue to adjudicate such … RIF appeals” (91 FR 51997). Section I.B says the Board “will accept such cases for filing where **the agency’s RIF notice was issued before the rule’s effective date**, and will not dismiss such appeals on the ground that OPM’s final rule displaced the MSPB’s jurisdiction” (91 FR 51997). Section III says the Board “will adjudicate any RIF appeals it receives after September 2, 2026, in which **the RIF effective date preceded September 2, 2026**” (91 FR 51998). The third trigger conflicts with the second and with OPM: OPM’s rule applies to a RIF action “for which an agency issues the employee a specific RIF notice … **on or after September 2, 2026**” (91 FR 49230, DATES), so a RIF noticed Aug. 1, 2026 with a Nov. 1, 2026 effective date is an OPM appeal and a Board appeal at the same time under Section III (and Section I.B puts it at the Board too), while a RIF noticed Sept. 10, 2026 with an effective date of Sept. 20, 2026 is an OPM appeal under OPM’s rule but not a Board appeal under Section III.
2. **“Rescission” of jurisdiction vs. retained adjudication.** The Board’s Summary says the rule removes references to Board jurisdiction over RIF appeals and “[t]his revision reflects [OPM’s] **rescission of the MSPB’s jurisdiction** to hear these types of appeals” (91 FR 51997), while the same document’s DATES and Section III state that the Board “will continue to adjudicate” RIF appeals not covered by OPM’s rule and will not dismiss them (91 FR 51997–98) — i.e., jurisdiction is discontinued prospectively only, with the line drawn by three different events as described above.

In (ii) I compared the full propose-versus-final regulatory texts; changes in (c)(3) of 351.901 (preserved forums now excluding the FLRA, which the proposal listed) were not listed because the final summary’s enumeration of preserved entities already tracks the final list.
